cards.title: Split packaging into product packaging (COGS) and shipping packaging (expense)
cards.summary: Distinguish the retail box that is part of the product from the transit box it ships in, since the two often arrive on one supplier invoice.
cards.use_when: When coding packaging supplier invoices, or when packaging spend is large enough to distort margin on fragile or gift-oriented products.

cards.title: Separate dropship product and shipping costs in margin analysis
cards.summary: Compare dropship and stocked orders on complete order contribution, with a documented accounting policy.
cards.use_when: When calculating margin for a drop-shipped product line, or when deciding whether to offer free shipping on a SKU.

cards.title: Code customer returns correctly and turn returns into a second sale
cards.summary: Classify the return cost accurately, then consider voucher or exchange offers that recover the sale — noting the extra accounting complexity they create.
cards.use_when: When managing return rates in apparel or other high-return categories, and when designing return-flow offers at the returns step.

cards.title: Capture freight and duty against the right purchase order at the time it happens
cards.summary: Stop accumulating unattributed freight and duty invoices; attach each cost to the purchase it belongs to so landed cost can actually be calculated.
cards.use_when: When inbound logistics costs are piling up unallocated, or when setting up the purchasing workflow for a growing ecommerce operation.

cards.title: Move from spreadsheets to weighted landed-cost allocation as SKU count grows
cards.summary: Attribute lump-sum freight and duty down to unit level so every SKU shows a true cost, using software once manual weighting becomes unreliable.
cards.use_when: When you sell many SKUs per shipment and cannot tell whether individual products are profitable, or when preparing to scale purchasing.

cards.title: Classify supplier discounts and credits against product cost
cards.summary: Reduce COGS when a supplier discounts goods you are buying; handle credits carefully where stock has moved back.
cards.use_when: When posting supplier credit notes, rebates or discounts and deciding whether they lower unit cost or sit as income.

cards.title: Troubleshoot a slipping P&L by reading upward, not sideways
cards.summary: Use the P&L hierarchy to locate which line above a missed target is causing the miss instead of guessing at an ads problem.
cards.use_when: Monthly or weekly review when net profit, contribution margin or gross margin misses target and you need to decide whether to cut spend, fix returns, reprice or renegotiate freight.

cards.title: Separate gross and net revenue to find hidden profit
cards.summary: Gross-to-net breakdown exposes refunds, discounts and shipping collected as the real revenue levers most accounting software hides.
cards.use_when: When revenue moved between two periods and you cannot explain it from marketing or OPEX, or when you are deciding where to hunt for margin before cutting ad spend.

cards.title: Recalculate contribution and break-even acquisition cost before discounting
cards.summary: Model discounted net revenue against all variable order costs before setting acquisition targets.
cards.use_when: Pricing and offer decisions — planning a promo, a bundle, a gift-with-purchase, or a clearance push, and setting the media efficiency target that promo must hit.

cards.title: Calculate pre-marketing contribution using explicit delivery costs
cards.summary: Separate accounting gross profit from the management contribution metric used to fund ecommerce acquisition.
cards.use_when: Before setting marketing KPIs on a product, deciding whether to keep or cut a SKU, or comparing your margin to competitor pricing.

cards.title: Split variable and fixed marketing costs inside the P&L
cards.summary: Media spend, influencer fees and agency retainers are variable (MEA); in-house creative teams are fixed (OPEX) — miscategorising either distorts contribution margin.
cards.use_when: Structuring your P&L for monthly review, or deciding whether to bring creative production in-house versus using agencies and freelancers.

cards.title: Waterfall pricing from bottom to top
cards.summary: Price by working from a contribution margin target through CAC, returns, fulfillment and COGS up to a price — then test it against competitors and cut the SKU if it fails.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, repricing an existing one, or evaluating whether a hero SKU can carry paid acquisition.

cards.title: Read product-level economics to beat maximize-conversions bidding
cards.summary: Per-product CAC versus contribution margin reveals which SKUs deserve paid spend, because default bidding optimises the cheapest CPA rather than the most profitable sale.
cards.use_when: Campaign structure and budget allocation decisions when a low-CPA product is absorbing spend while a higher-margin product under-sells.

cards.title: Geo-lift testing to measure true incremental spend
cards.summary: Select control and treatment regions, hold out spend, and compare actual revenue against predicted counterfactual revenue.
cards.use_when: When platform ROAS is untrustworthy and you need to decide how much more (or less) to spend in paid media, or validate a channel's real contribution before scaling budget.

cards.title: Forecast new and returning revenue as separate models
cards.summary: New customer revenue is driven by marketing inputs; returning revenue is driven by cohort decay rates and product launches — mixing them produces a forecast nobody can act on.
cards.use_when: Annual or quarterly planning, budget setting, or when deciding how hard to push acquisition versus retention investment.

cards.title: Fix CAC measurement before setting CAC targets
cards.summary: Use total ad spend divided by new customers, and pair CAC against first-purchase gross profit on new customers only.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition targets, reviewing agency performance, or diagnosing why a 'healthy' blended CAC is not producing profit.

cards.title: Separate new-customer and returning-customer profit contribution
cards.summary: Compute contribution margin on new and returning revenue separately to see where the business actually makes money.
cards.use_when: Deciding budget split between acquisition and retention, or when a founder wants to increase ad spend but the profit source is unclear.

cards.title: Measure 90/180-day LTGP, not open-ended LTV
cards.summary: Restrict customer value to a fixed window and use gross profit rather than revenue so acquisition bids are grounded.
cards.use_when: Setting maximum allowable CAC for CPG, fashion or subscription models where first-order profitability is negative or thin.

cards.title: Ring-fence OPEX to protect margin while scaling
cards.summary: In e-commerce the growth lever is marketing, not headcount or software, so overinflating OPEX flattens profit as revenue grows.
cards.use_when: Budget review when revenue is growing but net profit is flat in dollars, or when deciding whether to hire, add software or upsize an office.

cards.title: Use EBITDA and net profit as distinct decision numbers
cards.summary: Track EBITDA, net income and cash flow separately when financing inventory or planning owner distributions.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to take on inventory financing, setting owner distributions, or preparing numbers for a buyer or investor.

cards.title: Use product-level contribution margin to decide where paid spend goes
cards.summary: Break P&L economics down to the individual product so you can move ad budget from products that would sell anyway to products that need paid help.
cards.use_when: Deciding ad budget allocation across products, or whether a hero product should receive paid spend at all

cards.title: Measurement pyramid: platform metrics, finance-grade KPIs, incrementality
cards.summary: Rank your marketing metrics in a reliability pyramid — platform ROAS/CPA at the bottom, finance-grade KPIs in the middle, incrementality testing at the top.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing which marketing metrics you report on and make budget decisions from

cards.title: Why platform ROAS misleads: all attribution is correlation
cards.summary: Platform attribution connects correlated events, not causation, and systematically over-credits bottom-of-funnel — so ROAS misleads budget decisions.
cards.use_when: Interpreting channel-level ROAS reports or defending/attacking a channel's budget based on platform numbers

cards.title: Use finance-grade KPIs instead of platform-attributed numbers
cards.summary: Acquisition MER, blended MER, profit contribution and CAC calculate from actual new-customer revenue and actual ad spend, making them more reliable than platform metrics.
cards.use_when: Choosing which marketing efficiency numbers to report and act on for budget decisions

cards.title: Benchmark LTGP:CAC at fixed time horizons
cards.summary: LTGP to CAC contextualises acquisition cost with customer gross profit — but must be time-boxed (30, 90, sometimes 365 days) to avoid overspending on distant lifetime value.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition efficiency targets or auditing whether your CAC is defensible

cards.title: Exclude view-through conversions and existing customers from platform reporting
cards.summary: View-through conversions and existing-customer spend inflate platform ROAS — use 7-day click and check audience breakdowns and frequency.
cards.use_when: Configuring Meta attribution settings or auditing where ad budget is being spent

cards.title: Budget existing-customer retargeting from customer count × frequency, not a % of spend
cards.summary: Calculate existing-customer ad spend from number of existing customers × desired frequency × CPM rather than targeting a percentage of total budget.
cards.use_when: Setting retargeting/existing-customer budgets or responding to the question 'what % should go to existing customers?'

cards.title: The profit frontier: solve for the next best dollar
cards.summary: Allocate spend by finding the marginal return of the next $10,000 on each channel, and stop each channel where incremental acquisition MER hits break-even.
cards.use_when: Deciding incremental budget allocation across channels or whether to pull budget from one channel into another

cards.title: Grade inventory to drive paid-media decisions on slow-moving stock
cards.summary: Grade inventory A–D by sell-through and use paid media to liquidate grade B/C/D stock back into cash — a job profit-KPI'd agencies often ignore.
cards.use_when: Planning product launches, SKU rationalisation, or deciding whether to push clearance inventory through ads at break-even or a slight loss

cards.title: Cash conversion cycle explains why ecommerce can't scale arbitrarily fast
cards.summary: CCC (DIIO + DSO − DPO) plus supplier lead time and payment terms caps real growth speed regardless of ad efficiency.
cards.use_when: Setting growth targets, planning purchase orders, or evaluating whether rapid ad-spend scaling is fundable

cards.title: Resolve the CFO vs CMO spend-cut reflex with inventory reality
cards.summary: When unsold inventory is stuck, cutting media can deepen a revenue decline — sometimes the correct move is to raise MAR temporarily to liquidate stock.
cards.use_when: Responding to a cash squeeze or a CFO request to cut marketing budget when inventory isn't selling

cards.title: Forecast new-customer and returning-customer revenue separately
cards.summary: Forecast new and returning revenue as separate models because they have different underlying inputs — spend-driven vs cohort/event-driven.
cards.use_when: Building an ecommerce revenue forecast, budget or KPI target

cards.title: Build returning-customer forecasts from cohort repeat rates
cards.summary: Project next month's returning revenue by ageing every historical new-customer cohort through its average repeat rate and returning AOV, then adjusting for seasonality and events.
cards.use_when: Forecasting returning-customer revenue for next month's budget or board plan

cards.title: Model new-customer revenue by regression of spend vs acquisition MER
cards.summary: Plot daily spend against acquisition MER, strip outlier periods, fit a regression, and back-propagate from the new-customer revenue goal to see whether it's achievable.
cards.use_when: Forecasting new-customer revenue at a given spend level, or sanity-checking a growth target

cards.title: Don't overallocate to bottom-of-funnel because it shows the best ROAS
cards.summary: Bottom-of-funnel campaigns always show the best platform ROAS and top-of-funnel the worst, so shifting budget toward the 6x and away from the 2x usually reduces incremental growth.
cards.use_when: Reallocating budget between campaigns or channels based on platform ROAS reads

cards.title: Allocate part of marketing expense to brand, not just performance
cards.summary: Beyond roughly $1M–20M, performance marketing alone hits diminishing returns; brand associations built outside the ad account are what keep ad-account metrics strong at scale.
cards.use_when: Setting overall marketing budget allocation or planning acquisition strategy past a performance plateau

cards.title: Know your gross margin and variable costs as the base of all finance decisions
cards.summary: The source's first key takeaway: understand gross margin, how to calculate it correctly, and the difference between product margin and gross margin.
cards.use_when: Reviewing unit economics, setting pricing or acquisition targets, or preparing a P&L for a marketing decision

cards.title: Five core finance practices to run an ecommerce brand
cards.summary: A closing checklist of five financial operating habits—margin literacy, live dashboards, new/returning separation, cash vs P&L plays, and constraint diagnosis.
cards.use_when: Setting your store's monthly financial operating rhythm or auditing which finance disciplines your team is missing before scaling spend.

cards.title: Structure your P&L as a constraint-diagnosis tool
cards.summary: Read the P&L line by line, set KPIs at each level, and when a KPI drops look one level up to find the changed lever and correct course.
cards.use_when: When a store's profit or efficiency metric falls below target and you need to locate the actual constraint rather than reflexively cutting ad spend.

cards.title: Budget brand as a P&L expense line, not just performance marketing
cards.summary: High-quality brand associations, messaging and creative can drive purchases that performance ads would not, so brand deserves deliberate budget allocation.
cards.use_when: Deciding store budget allocation between performance marketing and brand-building (creative campaigns, positioning work) as you scale.

cards.title: Align marketing strategy with SKU inventory to prioritize cash turnover
cards.summary: When cash is the constraint, deliberately accept lower profitability or MER to move inventory into cash, coordinating marketing and inventory teams.
cards.use_when: Replenishment, pricing or promotion planning when a store is cash-constrained and holding slow-moving SKUs.

cards.title: Build a 48-month subscription financial model from ad spend down
cards.summary: Excel layout for forecasting a DTC subscription business: assumptions tab in blue, customer acquisition tab driving orders, then a monthly P&L out to 48 months.
cards.use_when: You need to plan store operations, model a raise, or test whether your ad budget and churn can produce a profitable subscription business before committing spend.

cards.title: Discounts vs CAC: when a discount is mathematically neutral
cards.summary: If a discount lifts conversion enough that CAC falls by the same dollar amount, post-marketing per-order contribution margin is unchanged — so discounting is a CAC substitute, not automatically a margin loss.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a discount or promo on a PDP, landing page or email flow, and whether the discount is actually cheaper than buying the same customers through paid ads.

cards.title: Split COGS into product and fulfillment to read ecommerce margins
cards.summary: Separate product cost from fulfillment cost instead of lumping them into one COGS line, so you can see product gross profit and fulfillment drag independently.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly store P&L, diagnosing why margins moved, or deciding whether a shipping, pick-and-pack or packaging decision is eroding profitability.

cards.title: Read a monthly P&L as percent of revenue to spot trajectory and margin drift
cards.summary: Lay revenue down through product cost, fulfillment, marketing and opex as percentages of revenue to see growth, margin predictability and where profitability broke.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly store review: assessing whether the business is growing, whether margins are stable, and which line caused a profitable month to turn into a loss.

cards.title: Compute per-order unit economics: AOV, product cost, fulfillment, contribution
cards.summary: Divide each P&L line by total orders to get AOV, product cost per order, fulfillment per order and contribution margin per order.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing whether each order is actually profitable before marketing, and comparing month-to-month stability of your order-level economics.

cards.title: Add per-unit product economics to find your most profitable SKU
cards.summary: Calculate revenue, product gross profit and contribution margin per unit for each top SKU, because blended per-order numbers hide product-mix differences.
cards.use_when: Product selection, pricing and merchandising decisions — deciding which SKUs to push, bundle or drop based on margin per unit rather than revenue share alone.

cards.title: Calculate blended CAC from total marketing and new customer orders
cards.summary: CAC/CPA is total marketing spend divided by new customer orders only — returning orders are excluded because they carry little paid marketing cost.
cards.use_when: Setting or auditing acquisition budgets, and comparing what you pay per new customer against the contribution margin that customer produces.

cards.title: Build customer retention cohorts to measure true repeat purchase behaviour
cards.summary: Group customers by first purchase month and track their orders over subsequent months to see real lifetime purchase frequency, not just first-month averages.
cards.use_when: Forecasting LTV, judging whether a subscription or replenishment offer is working, or deciding whether retention spend is justified by actual repeat behaviour.

cards.title: Define LTV as lifetime contribution margin and test it against CAC
cards.summary: Customer lifetime value is the total contribution margin a customer generates across their whole relationship — compare it to the marketing investment that acquired them to see if the model is profitable.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to scale ad spend, raise prices, launch a subscription, or accept a slower payback in exchange for profitable scale.

cards.title: Simplify a startup payroll model with salary x headcount ÷ 12
cards.summary: Forecast personnel cost from role salaries and headcount assumptions, plus a benefits load, instead of building a named-employee payroll.
cards.use_when: Building or updating the opex section of a startup or store financial model where you need a defensible payroll line without individual offer letters.

cards.title: Include an unallocated 'unknown' opex bucket
cards.summary: Reserve a percentage of revenue in the model for expenses you cannot yet name, so the forecast does not understate cash burn.
cards.use_when: Building the opex section of a store financial model or budget, especially pre-launch or when scaling into new channels with uncertain costs.

cards.title: Set up a quarterly roll-up with starting cash to calculate runway
cards.summary: A summary tab that sums quarters and years across a starting cash balance shows how long the business can operate before it needs more funding.
cards.use_when: Founder or investor reporting: answering how far a raised amount stretches, when cash turns negative, and which year the business becomes profitable.

cards.title: Format a financial model for fast reading: colours, brackets, freeze panes
cards.summary: Use consistent colour conventions, accounting format with zero-suppression, and freeze panes so a large model stays readable and auditable.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing any store P&L or financial model that others will read or edit.

cards.title: Build a standard VC-style 4-year model — and know its limits
cards.summary: Venture investors typically want about four years of monthly projections; the source demonstrates a 48-month model from a $3M raise for a coffee subscription.
cards.use_when: Preparing a data room or investor conversation, or stress-testing whether your store's plan supports the growth story a raise implies.

cards.title: Cohort Table Mechanics: Reading Repeat Orders Diagonally
cards.summary: How to build and read a customer cohort table so repeat revenue and lifetime order counts are calculated correctly.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a monthly cohort report to decide whether repeat-purchase revenue justifies acquisition spend.

cards.title: From First-Order Economics to Lifetime Value
cards.summary: Step-by-step build of first-order contribution margin, LTV, and the CM:CAC ratio so you can see whether acquisition pays back.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether current ad spend is profitable on a first-order and lifetime basis before scaling acquisition.

cards.title: Why 50% Off Sitewide Destroys Black Friday Unit Economics
cards.summary: The mechanical reason a sitewide percentage discount loses money even when traffic and conversion spike.
cards.use_when: Planning Black Friday or any sitewide promo and choosing between percentage discount and a multi-unit offer.

cards.title: BOGO / Two-for-One as a Black Friday Cash Machine
cards.summary: Replace sitewide percentage discounts with a two-for-one or gift-with-purchase to deliver perceived value without giving back revenue.
cards.use_when: Designing a seasonal promotion where you want the conversion lift of a deep discount but positive per-order profit.

cards.title: The Core Unit Economics Stack: CAC, AOV, CM, LTV and Their Ratios
cards.summary: Definitions and relationships for the five metrics that determine whether an ecommerce business model can work.
cards.use_when: Setting up your ecommerce financial model or explaining unit economics to your team before scaling spend.

cards.title: Two Valid Models: Break Even on Order One, or Lose Early and Earn Later
cards.summary: When it is safe to lose money on the first order and when you must be profitable on it.
cards.use_when: Deciding how aggressively to bid on acquisition for one-time-purchase versus repeat-purchase product lines.

cards.title: Ecom Gross Margin vs Contribution Margin: Two Different Buckets
cards.summary: Separating product-level costs from per-order fulfillment costs so you know which costs scale with each order and which vary by shipment.
cards.use_when: Building your P&L model or diagnosing why margin differs between orders and shipping destinations.

cards.title: Healthy Unit Economics Benchmarks Across the Business Lifecycle
cards.summary: How CAC, AOV, contribution margin and lifetime orders typically move from idea stage to late stage in a strong business.
cards.use_when: Benchmarking your own unit economics against a stage-appropriate expectation before raising or deploying growth capital.

cards.title: Sub-Optimal Pattern: Rising CAC With Flat Contribution Margin
cards.summary: The failure mode where a business scales spend faster than it fixes economics, losing money on every customer.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether an influx of funding should be spent on more acquisition or on fixing supply chain and retention first.

cards.title: Splitting COGS Into Product and Fulfillment Buckets for Promo Modeling
cards.summary: The two-bucket COGS structure used to compare promotions and normal trading side by side.
cards.use_when: Building a promo P&L for Black Friday, bundles or free shipping tests, or recalculating contribution margin per order.

cards.title: Three-Statement Model as the Diagnostic for a Profitable-but-Cash-Poor Store
cards.summary: Why ecommerce stores show positive net income and falling cash, and which statement lines to inspect in order.
cards.use_when: Investigating why your store's bank balance declines in months when the P&L shows profit.

cards.title: Balance Sheet Cash Traps: Inventory, Capitalized Software, Quarterly Taxes
cards.summary: The three balance-sheet movements that most often explain cash going out while the P&L looks healthy.
cards.use_when: Planning a buying season, an engineering spend, or a tax payment quarter and forecasting whether cash can support it.

cards.title: Reading the Cash Flow Statement: Operating, Investing, Financing
cards.summary: How each section of the cash flow statement maps to ecommerce activity so you can trace where cash actually moves.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly cash movements and classifying spend the way a lender or investor will read it.

cards.title: Diagnosing Gross Margin Drops During Promo Months
cards.summary: Tracking gross margin percentage month over month to catch discount-driven margin erosion separate from volume effects.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly performance after a sale event to see whether volume gains were bought with margin.

cards.title: Free cash flow vs net income: inventory and tax timing as cash drivers
cards.summary: Read the cash flow statement to see why free cash flow diverges from net income, driven mainly by inventory build/sell-through and tax payment timing.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly cash review for your store, especially when net income looks positive but your bank balance is falling, or you are deciding how much inventory to buy for the next selling season.

cards.title: Calculate contribution margin per order and post-marketing contribution
cards.summary: Structure an ecommerce P&L into net revenue, product COGS, gross margin, fulfillment, contribution margin, CAC and post-marketing contribution so each expense can be optimized separately.
cards.use_when: Setting or reviewing product-level and order-level profitability, or diagnosing why a store that looks profitable at gross margin is not producing operating income.

cards.title: Treat discount and CAC as one acquisition cost pool
cards.summary: Discounts and marketing spend are mathematically equivalent per-customer costs, so combine them into a single budget and optimize the split for total profit, not per-customer margin.
cards.use_when: Planning next quarter's promotional calendar and ad budget, or deciding whether a deeper discount or more ad spend will grow profit for the whole store.

cards.title: Price prepaid bundles by comparing margin loss against retention gain
cards.summary: Prepaid multi-order bundles cut per-order margin but lock in multiple orders, so evaluate them on total lifetime profit rather than the discounted order's gross profit alone.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch or expand 3/6/12-order prepaid bundles, subscribe-and-save tiers, or any offer that trades discount depth for committed repeat orders.

cards.title: Build separate unit economics for transactional vs subscription customers
cards.summary: Transactional and subscription customers have different AOVs, discounts and cost structures, so model their unit economics on separate rows before forecasting any revenue.
cards.use_when: Building or rebuilding a subscription-box or subscribe-and-save financial model, or deciding whether subscription revenue is actually more profitable than your ad hoc channel.

cards.title: Forecast ad spend divided by CAC to drive new customer counts
cards.summary: In a subscription-box model, marketing spend is the master lever: ad spend divided by CAC yields new customers, and everything downstream flows from it.
cards.use_when: Building a 36-month growth forecast, sizing cash needs or runway, or testing how sensitive your plan is to CAC improvements.

cards.title: Turn a contribution-margin model into a pricing and negotiation checklist
cards.summary: Because net margin per order is thin, identify each controllable line — freight, duties, pick and pack, packaging, 3PL, payment fees — and quantify what a dollar saved on each is worth at your order volume.
cards.use_when: Negotiating with a 3PL, carrier or supplier, evaluating a packaging change, or deciding where to spend optimization effort in an ecommerce P&L.

cards.title: Define gross margin, contribution margin and post-marketing contribution consistently
cards.summary: Treat gross margin, contribution margin and post-marketing contribution as three distinct measures with different purposes, and use contribution margin as the base you optimize back from.
cards.use_when: Setting up your store's reporting definitions, briefing an analyst or account manager, or comparing your margins against others' quoted figures.

cards.title: Build a Linked Acquisition-to-Retention Model for Transactional + Subscription Mix
cards.summary: Forecast ad-hoc and subscription customer streams separately so you can see how each drives revenue, profit and LTV in a blended subscription business.
cards.use_when: Financial planning for a store selling both one-time purchases and subscriptions (subscription box, supplements, consumables) where you need to model growth, breakeven and cash needs.

cards.title: Forecast Marketing Spend into New Customers via CAC Assumptions
cards.summary: Convert a monthly ad budget into expected new customers by dividing spend by an assumed and iteratively updated CAC.
cards.use_when: Setting or pressure-testing monthly ad spend and growth targets for a store, and checking whether the acquired customers can ever be profitable.

cards.title: Use Trigger Events to Shift New Customers from One-Time to Subscription
cards.summary: Sequence offer, discount and cart-default changes over months to lift the subscription share of new customers toward a 30/70 steady state.
cards.use_when: Designing subscription upsell offers, discount structures and cart/checkout defaults for a store trying to move from mostly one-time sales to recurring revenue.
